chemical formula ABX3 (A = Cs, formamidinium (FA), or
methylammonium (MA); B = Pb or Sn; X = Br, Cl, or I), have
attracted great interest from experts due to their extraordinary

adjustable band gaps.1,2 Since the band gap directly affects the
range of the solar spectrum that the HOIPs can absorb, it plays

the composition atomic ratios and the band gap using the
SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) method, which
provided “a posteriori” explanation for the model. However,
this interpretability is based on ion concentration, and
although it can provide guidance for band gap regulation in
this system, it neither reflects the effect of physical parameters
on the band gap, nor extends it to band gap prediction for
other doping systems. For example, the case of trace doping of
other metal ions in Pb-based HOIPs.
In order to physically explain the factors that affect the band
gap, researchers introduce domain knowledge and construct
features with physical meaning as model inputs. Wu et al.12
predicted the band gap of mixed double halide organic−
inorganic perovskites (MDHOIPs) by taking physical features
such as the ionic radius (IR) and electronegativity as model
inputs based on DFT calculated data. They found that the B-
site ion radius and electronegativity have an important effect
on the band gap by the feature importance ranking of GBRT.
Im et al.13 established a GBRT model to predict the band gap
of double perovskite with the structure A2B1+B3+X6 based on
DFT calculated data. By ranking the feature importance scores
of the GBRT model, it was found that the main factors
affecting the band gap of double perovskite are the space group
of crystal and Pauling’s electronegativity of the X-site.
Although the use of physical features increases the
interpretability of the model, limited by the “black box”
problem of ML models, it is only a qualitative interpretation of
factors affecting the band gap and cannot intuitively reflect the
quantitative relationship between the band gap and physical
features.
Genetic algorithm-based symbolic regression (GASR)
provides a new way to solve the “black box” problem of ML
by obtaining mathematical formulas that quantify the relation-
ships between features and predictive properties (labels) by
mathematical formulas.14 Weng et al.15 used the GASR
algorithm to identify a simple formula 1.554
+1.092 for
describing the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) activity of
oxide perovskite catalysts, where μ and τ are the octahedral
and tolerance factors, respectively. This new formula enables
rapid discovery of a series of new oxide perovskite catalysts
with improved OER activities. The use of the GASR method
provides insight into the interpretable prediction of the
perovskite band gap. However, there is very little work on
the use of the GASR algorithm for experimental band gap
prediction work for HOIPs at present.

band gap prediction, the focus of this work is to predict the
experimental band gap values of HOIPs using an interpretable
ML strategy. The flowchart is illustrated in Figure 1. A data set
consisting of HOIPs’ experimental band gaps was used to build
ML models. After that, we constructed an interpretable ML
strategy to improve the physical interpretability of the model in
three parts: First, based on feature engineering, physical
properties such as average electronegativity and average IR
were used to replace the composition atomic ratio as a feature
to facilitate the acquisition of physical interpretations. Next,
the GBRT algorithm was used to construct a high-performance
prediction model and explain the importance of the feature.
Finally, using the GASR algorithm allowed clear mathematical
formulations to be obtained for quantitative analysis of the
band gaps. We validated our predictions experimentally by
performing measurements on three novel HOIPs screened

■METHODS
Data Preparation. To ensure the quantity and accuracy of the
data, two principles were used in the data collection and cleaning
process. First, we selected compounds with a three-dimensional
structure of ABX3 (A-site = Cs, FA, or MA; B-site = Pb or Sn; X-site =
Br, Cl, or I). Second, for data with the same composition but different
band gaps, we chose the average value when the difference between
the maximum value and the minimum value is less than 0.2 eV. When
it is greater than 0.2 eV, we chose the model because the experimental
error is about 0.1−0.2 eV when using different instruments. All data
points were collated from the PSC database built by Jacobsson et al.16
Eventually, the total data set consists of 610 data points with known
band gap values. To assess the uncertainty of the data set, we
calculated the standard deviation of 352 data points with the same
composition but different band gaps reported by different literature.
The resulting probability density distribution of the standard
deviation of band gaps is shown in Figure S1a, with an average
standard deviation of 0.0134 eV and a 95th percentile value of 0.068
eV, which quantifies the level of uncertainty in the data to a certain
extent. Then, we randomly divided 15% of the data set as the test set
to evaluate the generalization capability for all ML models, and the
remaining 85% as the training set to train all ML models. All data are
visible in Tables S1 and S2 in the Supporting Information. The
probability density distribution plots of band gap in the training set
and the test set are shown in Figures S1b,c, indicating that they have
similar distributions and that the testing data set was partitioned
appropriately. In the training data set, the band gap is mainly
distributed between 1.5 and 1.6 eV, which has been extensively
studied. The data quantity is limited in the wide band gap range
greater than 2.5 eV, particularly for Cl-containing compounds, which
have been less studied. Interestingly, the addition of Cl can
significantly increase the band gap value.10,11
Feature Engineering and Model Construction. In order to
validate the accuracy of the data set and comparison with the
subsequent model with physical features as input, we simultaneously
trained models with composition (ML-C) as features using multiple
algorithms, including GBRT, ANN, k-nearest neighbor (KNN),
support vector regression (SVR), and the 10-fold cross-validation grid
search was used to find the optimal parameters for all the ML models.
They are named GBRT-C, ANN-C, KNN-C, and SVR-C. They all use
eight elemental atomic ratios as feature inputs, which are Cs, FA, MA,
Pb, Sn, Br, Cl, and I, where the atomic ratio of each site sums to 1.
The model performances are shown in Table S3, where GBRT-C has
the highest accuracy, and the RMSE of the test set is 0.046 eV, which
is currently the highest accuracy compared to the work of Li and Liu
mentioned earlier.10,11
To further enhance the physical interpretability, we used physical
features to replace the simple atomic ratio features as the model
inputs (ML-P). Previous works have shown that the excellent model’s
performance can be obtained by employing electronic properties-
related and structure-related features such as electronegativity,
Goldschmidt tolerance factor (τ), and octahedral factor (μ).12,13,17
In this work, we chose nine element characteristics as descriptors in
the initial feature pool based on a priori knowledge, including
Pauling’s electronegativity (χ), μ, τ, IR, electron affinity (EA), dipole
polarizability (DP), atomic radius (AR), and the number of electrons
on d and f orbitals. The A-site cations contain organic molecules, so
just the IR feature was used. Meanwhile, all features and descriptions
are shown in Table S4. In addition to the individual descriptors, we
considered their sums, differences, and ratios to create new features,
named feature crosses; details are given in the Supporting
Information, and Pauling’s electronegativity used for the elements
of B-site and X-site is given in Table S5. The arithmetic operators:
addition, subtraction, and division, were used to create new features
for the feature of IR, and only subtraction was used to create new
features for all initial features except IR. Finally, 27 new features were
generated.
When the model input contains many highly correlated features, it
will increase the dimensionality of the feature space and lead to
unnecessary complexity in the resulting model. In order to reduce
model complexity to improve the model accuracy and to reduce the
model training time, we reduced the dimensionality of the new
features in two steps. First step, we subject these features to a
correlation filter to classify the highly correlated features by Pearson
correlation coefficient analysis, which can be used to quantify the
linear correlation between features and retain complete feature
information. The Pearson correlation coefficient between features is
shown in Figure S2 and the Pearson correlation coefficient is defined

■RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
Feature Importance. Figure 3a shows the feature
importance generated by the GBRT-P model, where the top
ranked features are mainly associated with B-site cations and
X-site anions, proving that these two site elements play a
crucial role in the band gap. In particular, the electronegativity
difference between the B-site and the X-site (χB−X), the EA
potential difference between the B-site and the X-site (EAB−X),
and the octahedral factor μ are the three most important
features. These results are consistent with the Pearson
correlation coefficient matrix between features (Figure S2),
which demonstrates that these three features have the
strongest linear correlation with the band gap. Previous studies
have shown that the valence band maximum is mainly
contributed by the B-site s-orbital and the X-site p-orbital,
and the conduction band minimum is formed by the B-site p-
orbital and the X-site s-orbital.18 Thus, the band gap is mainly
determined by the B-site cation and X-site anion together,
which agrees with the ML results. Moreover, Figure 3a shows
that χB−X is the most important feature, which has been proved
to be a very important feature affecting the band gap in
previous studies using DFT data to train ML models.19,20 The
two-dimensional scatter plot of the χB−X and band gaps in
Figure S4a shows that the band gap increases with the increase
of χB−X, which is consistent with the results of previous DFT
calculations,21 that is, a larger electronegativity difference
between the B-site cation and the X-site anion tends to a larger
band gap. We note that EAB−X is second only to χB−X in
importance. EA is the amount of energy required to detach one
electron from a negatively charged ion of an atom or a
molecule. It is similar to the definition of electronegativity, and
the two are highly correlated (Figure S2), which explains why
it ranks relatively high. According to the rules for the
contribution of ion orbitals to the band-edge, the number of
electrons in the d orbital at the X-site (dX) does not contribute,
but the feature appears in the middle of the order of feature
importance. By comparing the orbitals of the X-site (dCl = 0,
dBr = 10, dI = 10), it is found that only Cl is without d orbital
electrons, so the dX here may be mainly used to distinguish
whether a compound contains Cl ions or not.
In addition to elemental features, the feature importance
ranking also proves that the structural feature (μ) has a
significant effect on the band gap, which can reflect the degree
of distortion of the [BX6] octahedral framework. Furthermore,
both DFT calculations and experiments demonstrate that the
octahedral tilt will lead to an increase in the band gap.22,23
Figure S4c shows the two-dimensional scatter plot of the μ and
band gaps, which shows that the band gap increases linearly
with μ. The regular octahedron will be obtained when the
value of μ is 0.414,6 and as this value increases, the octahedral
tilt increases. Therefore, it can be considered that the band gap
increases with the tilt of the octahedra [BX6]. Moreover, it can
be found that the feature importance ranking for the A-site
cations is very far back, indicating that the A-site cations may
have little effect on the band gaps. In order to exclude that this
is a result due to the A-site feature including only the IR, we

■CONCLUSIONS
In this work, we combined the GBRT and GASR algorithm to
propose an interpretable ML strategy for predicting the
experimental band gaps of HOIPs and identifying the key
factors that affect the band gap. By employing physical features
instead of simple atomic ratio features, the physical influence
factors for band gap were revealed, and the GBRT algorithm
with an RMSE error of prediction below 0.06 eV was
established. The feature importance analysis revealed that the
difference in electronegativity between the B-site and the X-site
χB−X is the most critical factor affecting band gaps, which is a
semitransparent interpretation, Further, we employed the
GASR algorithm to establish the mathematical formula Eg =
χB−X
2 + 0.881χB−X to fully transparently interpret the
relationship between physical features and band gaps. Three
new compositions were synthesized by model screening,
among which MA0.23FA0.02Cs0.75Pb0.59Sn0.41Br0.24I2.76 has an
ideal band gap of 1.39 eV. As a result, our interpretable ML
strategy created by combining physical features and GBRT and
GASR algorithms were successfully applied to develop HOIPs
with desirable band gaps and can be applied to a wider range of
materials.
